topic: pickling cucumbers in brine: salt by weight, surface yeast, weighting under the brine and keeping them crisp

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-6)
provenance.notes: pisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: waga warsztatowa odwazajaca sol do kazdej solanki

base: I have started pickling cucumbers in brine and the first crock went soft after ten days.
An old crock stands in the pantry and my grandmother used it every autumn for cabbage.
A bench scale sits beside it and weighs out the salt for every batch I mix.
I used two spoonfuls of salt to a litre of water and left the crock in the kitchen.
Was that too little salt, or is softening simply what happens in warm weather?
Too little salt, and the warmth of the kitchen finished what the weak brine had begun.
Weigh the salt rather than measure it, since spoonfuls vary by half depending on the grain.
Three per cent of the weight of the water is the usual strength for cucumbers.
Softening comes from the wrong bacteria, which weak brine and warm rooms both encourage.
I weighed the salt properly this time and mixed the brine to three per cent.
The bench scale makes that easy, and the second crock has stayed firm for a fortnight.
A white film has formed on the surface and smells rather like old bread to me.
Should I throw the batch out, or is that film something I can simply skim away?
Skim it away, since a white film of that kind is a surface yeast and not a spoilage.
It grows where the brine meets the air and does no harm below the surface at all.
Skim every second day and wipe the sides of the crock down to the brine line.
Blue or black growth is another matter entirely and means the whole batch goes out.
I skimmed every second day and the film stopped coming back after the first week.
Some cucumbers near the top had risen above the brine and gone slimy on one side.
The old crock has a stone weight with it that I had not thought to use.
I have been holding the vegetables down with a plate and a jam jar of water.
Is a proper weight worth having, or will the plate do exactly the same work?
A plate will do, provided nothing floats past its edge and up into the air.
The stone weight is better because it covers the whole surface and cannot tip sideways.
Anything that rises above the brine will spoil, however good the brine beneath it is.
Add a cabbage leaf under the weight as well, which catches whatever works its way up.
Keep the level a good two fingers above the vegetables and top it up as it falls.
I used the stone weight with a cabbage leaf beneath it and lost nothing at all.
The cucumbers are sour now and taste right, though they are softer than shop ones.
Someone at the market told me to add oak or blackcurrant leaves to the crock.
Does that really keep them crisp, or is it a story people tell each other?
It works, and the reason is tannin, which slows the softening of the vegetable wall.
Oak, blackcurrant, cherry and horseradish leaves all carry enough tannin to matter here.
Two or three leaves to a five litre crock is plenty, and more makes them bitter.
Cutting the flower end off each cucumber helps as much, since the softening starts there.
Oak leaves and trimming the flower end together made a very great difference indeed.
The crock is finished and I would like to keep the next lot until the spring.
My kitchen never falls below eighteen degrees, even in the coldest part of winter.
Where should a crock be kept once the souring has gone as far as I want?
Cold is the whole answer, and anywhere under six degrees will hold them for months.
A cellar, an unheated porch or the bottom of a cold larder will all serve.
Souring never stops entirely, but at that temperature it slows to almost nothing.
Move them across as soon as the taste is right, since another warm week undoes it.
